analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run health insurance program covering all Americans, funded by new taxes and drug price controls.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 25 cosponsors in the House in May 2019, was referred to six committees and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Medicare for America Act would have created a national government health insurance program covering every U.S. resident, including dental, vision, hearing, and long-term care. People would pay income-based premiums capped at 8% of income, with no deductibles and out-of-pocket costs capped at $3,500 per person or $5,000 per household. It would have banned most private insurance that duplicates the public plan, required the government to negotiate drug prices and cap prices it deems excessive, and paid for it with new taxes, including a surtax and excise taxes on tobacco, alcohol, and sugary drinks. The bill was referred to six House committees and never advanced; it died without a hearing or vote when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident would gain guaranteed, comprehensive coverage — including dental, vision, hearing, and home- and community-based long-term care — with no deductibles, an out-of-pocket cap of $3,500 per person or $5,000 per household, zero premiums for households below 200% of the poverty line, and premiums capped at 8% of income above that [S3]. Workers who today can lose coverage by changing or losing a job would instead carry a public card automatically; people with disabilities would get Medicare immediately instead of waiting 24 months; and small employers could enroll workers without a mandatory contribution [S3]. Members of Congress and their staff would be enrolled in the same program [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: All U.S. residents, especially the uninsured and low-income

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a national health insurance program administered by HHS that covers all U.S. residents, including hospital services, prescription drugs, dental services, and home- and community-based long-term care.

Eliminates deductibles, bans balance billing and surprise billing, and caps out-of-pocket costs at $3,500 per person or $5,000 per household, with zero out-of-pocket costs and zero premiums for households below 200% of the poverty line [S3].

Bans private insurers from selling plans that duplicate Medicare for America's benefits, ends prior authorization and step therapy for covered services, and lets people keep private coverage only for benefits the program does not cover [S3].

Prohibits excessive prices for prescription drugs and medical devices through a newly established federal review board, and authorizes the government to negotiate drug prices and license competing manufacture when negotiation fails [S2][S3].
Ends the 24-month waiting period for Medicare coverage of people with disabilities and eliminates Medicaid waiting-list periods, and guarantees abortion coverage without state restriction [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Higher-income households and investors would pay through a new surtax, changes to Medicare payroll and net investment income taxes, and repeal of the 2017 tax law [S3]. Smokers, drinkers, and sugary-drink consumers would pay new or higher excise taxes [S3]. Private insurers would lose the ability to sell plans duplicating the public program's benefits [S3]; drug manufacturers would face negotiated prices, an 'excessive price' prohibition enforced by a new federal review board, and possible government-licensed generic competition [S2][S3]. Employers could no longer offer coverage duplicating the public plan and would face a firm-wide contribution if they opted out of offering insurance [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill is financed by a broad set of new taxes, including a surtax, changes to Medicare payroll and net investment income taxes, higher taxes on tobacco and alcohol, and a new tax on sugared drinks [S3], which would raise costs for consumers and businesses.
The bill sunsets Public Law 115-97 (the 2017 tax law) [S2][S3], reversing a wide range of tax changes beyond health care, a choice that would have faced significant opposition on its own.

The transition would be disruptive: the bill sunsets the ACA exchanges in 2022 and phases out traditional Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP between 2023 and 2027 [S3], requiring tens of millions of people and employers to switch coverage over several years.

The government would take on a large new long-term care benefit covering home and community-based services for anyone unable to perform daily activities [S3], a benefit whose long-run cost no independent estimate in the record addresses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits would have been large for most households: guaranteed coverage including dental, vision, hearing, and long-term care, no deductibles, caps on out-of-pocket costs, and protection from medical debt and surprise billing. The costs are real and serious: the plan would be financed by a broad package of tax increases (surtax, investment taxes, tobacco, alcohol, and sugary drink excise taxes) and by redirecting Medicare and Medicaid spending, so the burden falls substantially on higher earners, investors, and consumers of taxed goods. Even many supporters of universal coverage considered a transition of this scale risky, and the bill's hybrid design — retaining private Medicare Advantage plans and employer coverage — drew criticism from both single-payer advocates (for not eliminating private insurance) and opponents (for expanding government's role). The bill never received a committee hearing or vote, so it was never costed or debated in earnest, and the country never got to weigh these trade-offs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to six House committees, assigned to subcommittees, and then sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the Medicare for America Act of 2019 in the House on May 1, 2019, with 16 original cosponsors [S3].
The bill was referred to six House committees — Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, Judiciary, Natural Resources, and House Administration [S1][S5].
Within a month it was split among three subcommittees (Health; Indigenous Peoples; Courts, Intellectual Property, and the Internet) [S5].
No committee ever reported the bill and no floor vote ever occurred; its last recorded action is the May 2019 subcommittee referrals [S5].
It never gained traction beyond 25 Democratic cosponsors — about one in nine House Democrats — and had no Republican cosponsors [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, private health insurers, pharmaceutical companies, and employers who would have faced new taxes and mandates keep the status quo; Americans without affordable coverage gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and drug makers; status quo persisted

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 1, 2019 and recruited 15 original cosponsors [S1][S3].

for.name: 25 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all cosponsors were Democrats, about one in nine of the Democratic caucus [S4].

against.name: House committee and subcommittee leadership
against.role: Chairs of Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, Judiciary, Natural Resources, and House Administration
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred to their committees; the record shows no action beyond subcommittee referrals [S5].

against.name: All 197 of 197 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the 197 House Republicans cosponsored the bill [S4].

against.name: Health insurance and pharmaceutical industries
against.what_they_did: Opposed national health insurance proposals that would ban duplicate private coverage and cap drug prices, through public lobbying and advertising campaigns against Medicare-for-all-style legislation.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 cosponsors were Democrats and none of the 197 House Republicans signed on; the bill's inaction reflected majority-party priorities as much as Republican opposition [S4].

industries.note: The bill bans insurers from selling plans that duplicate the public program's benefits, ending their core business in the individual and much of the employer market; they could offer only supplemental coverage or a rebranded Medicare Advantage product paid 95% of public rates [S3]. Their gain would have come at the cost of coverage and affordability for ordinary people.

The bill requires HHS to negotiate drug prices, lets a review board cap prices and devices deemed excessive, and authorizes the government to override patents and license generic manufacture when negotiations fail [S2][S3]. Cheaper drugs for patients come directly out of manufacturer revenues.

The bill locks providers into the public program — all Medicare and Medicaid providers automatically participate — while paying hospitals at least 110% of Medicare rates and raising primary care and behavioral health rates by at least 30% [S3]. Providers keep large public revenue streams under a single-channel system.

Rather than ending Medicare Advantage, the bill converts it into 'Medicare Advantage for America,' letting private insurers keep selling managed plans within the public program, paid 95% of public costs [S3]. Private insurers retain a guaranteed role in the public system.

Employers could either keep qualifying coverage or pay a firm-wide contribution and enroll workers in the public plan; large employers would shift to the public program starting in 2027 [S3]. Many employers would shed a costly benefit obligation.
New excise taxes on cigarettes, alcohol, and sugared drinks [S3] would raise costs for these industries and for consumers of their products.
